market_context: United States/general English; hake treated as multiple species with raw and cooked values clearly separated
title: Hake: protein, fat, calories, and nutrition

seo.title: Hake nutrition: protein, fat, calories, and nutrients
seo.meta_description: Hake is a very lean white fish. Depending on species, raw hake can be roughly 65–90 calories, 12–18 g protein and 1–2 g fat per 100 g.
seo.search_intent: Understand hake nutrition and why values change by species, raw versus cooked state, and preparation.

excerpt: Hake is among the leaner fish choices: different raw species can range roughly from 65 to 90 calories and 1–2 grams fat per 100 grams. Protein may appear anywhere from about 12 to 18 grams because “hake” is not one species or one database entry.
content_html:
Hake is commonly treated as one white fish, but the name covers multiple species and nutrition tables do not always describe the same fish. Ranges are therefore more honest than one universal number.

Approximate raw nutrition per 100 g

NutrientTypical range
Calories~65–90
Protein~12–18 g
Fat~1–2 g
Carbohydrate0 g

NOAA’s current red hake reference lists 90 calories, 18.31 g protein, and 1.31 g fat per 100 g raw. European hake entries for other species can land closer to 65 calories and 12 g protein.

Hake is genuinely lean

At roughly 1–2 g fat/100 g, hake is far leaner than Atlantic salmon, which commonly provides around 10–13 g fat/100 g. The gap can be roughly 9–12 g fat and 90–145 calories per 100 g.

That does not make salmon nutritionally worse; its additional fat also carries much more EPA and DHA.

Cooked protein looks higher because water is lost

A raw hake entry with 18 g protein/100 g can move above 20 g/100 g after cooking. Cooking does not create protein; it reduces water and concentrates the remaining solids.

That is why comparing raw hake with roasted salmon without stating the food state produces a misleading protein comparison.

A serving can provide substantial protein

If cooked hake lands around 20–23 g protein/100 g, a 5-ounce serving can provide roughly 28–33 g protein while remaining relatively low in calories when little fat is added.

Cooking fat can matter more than the fish

Steaming, baking, poaching, or lightly pan-cooking keeps hake lean. Ten grams of oil adds about 90 calories, and breading plus deep frying can add considerably more.

Does hake contain omega-3?

Yes, but much less than fatty fish. Hake species generally contain long-chain omega-3 in tenths of a gram per 100 g, while Atlantic salmon references often provide around 1.8–2.2 g EPA+DHA/100 g.

Selenium is another useful nutrient

NOAA lists 32.1 mcg selenium and 72 mg natural sodium per 100 g raw red hake. Exact micronutrients vary by species, but lean protein plus selenium and B vitamins is a common white-fish pattern.

The useful takeaway

Hake is a high-protein, very low-fat fish. Raw references range roughly 65–90 calories, 12–18 g protein, and 1–2 g fat per 100 g. For one precise number, check the species, raw/cooked state, and whether oil or breading is part of the preparation.

faq.question: How much protein is in hake?
faq.answer: Depending on species and state, roughly 12–18 g/100 g raw; cooked hake can exceed 20 g/100 g because water is lost.

faq.question: Is hake low in fat?
faq.answer: Yes. Raw hake commonly contains only about 1–2 g fat per 100 g.

faq.question: How many calories does hake have?
faq.answer: Raw species references often range from roughly 65 to 90 calories per 100 g; cooking oil and breading change the final dish.
